abstract: Eastern redcedar (Juniperus virginiana L., Cupressaceae; ERC) is rapidly expanding throughout the Great Plains. However, its effects on woodlands, particularly in the Northern Great Plains, are poorly understood, even as managers invest substantially in its removal. To fill this gap, along an ERC dominance gradient in a forest inventory plot in Nebraska, we assessed: (1) how woodland understory plant communities and environmental conditions varied and (2) where and how ERC management had the greatest benefits. Spatial neighborhood analyses showed that greater ERC canopy reduced woody seedling abundance, species richness, and species diversity relative other canopy species. No canopy species, including ERC, was associated with variation in herbaceous species richness. ERC dominance was unrelated to soil moisture, pH, or organic matter, but was associated with reduced understory light, suggesting that dense ERC foliage limits seedling establishment. Simulated management scenarios predicted that continued encroachment would shift the woody understory community toward disturbance-tolerant shrubs and away from canopy tree species, likely altering forest structural and species diversity and reducing habitat quality. ERC removal at low to moderate encroachment levels and from steep canyon habitats was associated with the greatest increases in seedling abundance and species richness, but also small declines in diversity, with implications for the complex decisions of when, where, and how much of this native species to remove. Our results indicate that ERC encroachment has reduced woody species diversity, and left unchecked, will likely continue to do so, with potentially cascading effects on higher trophic levels, biotic interactions, and ecosystem services.
